newsitem.title: CANADA: Rural Canadians embrace boom, flex economic muscle.
newsitem.headline: Rural Canadians embrace boom, flex economic muscle.

text.p: Rural Canadians are the foot servants of Canada's resource-based economy, a role that earns them lower incomes, fewer jobs and a dependency on social programmes.
Recently, however, small islands of prosperity have been emerging and transforming former backwaters into boomtowns.

For many of the 9.7 million rural Canadians -- defined by Canada's statistical agency, Statistics Canada, as those living outside big cities -- the economic upturn is nothing short of revolutionary. Canada's total population is 30 million.
Winkler, Manitoba, a predominantly Mennonite community that clings to the tenets of church, family and kinship, is one spoke in the wheel of the rural economy.
Thirty years ago, Winkler, 20 miles (32.19 km) from the North Dakota border, was a typical farm town, its residents dependent on the vicissitudes of agriculture.

Today the town's 7,000 residents are profiting from a boom in the holy trinity -- agriculture, manufacturing and the service sector. Unemployment in the town is flat at three percent. Credit is plenty.

"A lot of rural communities died because they counted on agriculture to support them. We were saved because we have this excellent industrial growth side and a growing service side," says Terry Elias, president of Triple E Canada Ltd., the largest Canadian manufacturer of recreational vehicles.
Triple E is credited by many in the community for launching the Winkler wake-up in the 1960s.

In that era of rural flight, company founder Peter Enns acted on an idea rooted in an earlier mission in India, where he became enamoured with the relative comfort and affordability of mobile trailers.
Enlisting the aid of his two sons-in-law, Enns began building a prototype. Within two years, Triple E was selling more than 300 vehicles a year throughout Canada.
The company spawned an entire cottage industry of parts manufacturers -- from cabinet makers to welding shops.

"They (Triple E) put Winkler on the map because their units were going out all over Canada," said Henry Wiebe, who served as mayor of the town from 1967 to 1991. "They have given good employment directly and indirectly to hundreds of people in the community."
Winkler is by no means the only rural success story.

In Steinbach, Manitoba, about 100 miles (160.9 km) northeast of Winkler, the local credit union is awash with cash -- partly due to the high agricultural prices of the past two years -- and officials are in the peculiar pickle of not knowing how to unleaven the coffers.

"The problem isn't that they have no businesses to lend to, but that so much savings and wealth is being created in the town," said Ray Bollman, a research economist with Statistics Canada and a visiting fellow at the Rural Development Institute in Brandon, Manitoba.
While Winkler and Steinbach entered the industrial economy with little infrastructure in place, other towns have made the leap through a rebirth of manufacturing.

Coaticook, Quebec, near the Vermont border, was a thriving textile town until Asian competitors took over the market. Today, the town is one of the world's largest manufacturers of firehoses and a regular supplier of rubber moulding for Toyota's North American auto plants.
Whether industrialising for the first time, like Winkler, or re-industrialising, like Coaticook, rural boomtowns share some common threads.

A reliance on small business as the vehicle for growth is one common foundation. Rural areas have almost twice the share of their employees in small businesses compared to urban businesses, according to Statistics Canada.

Similarly, the rate of job loss among larger businesses in rural areas is half the rate of larger urban businesses. Rural industry has taken off because local conditions and needs have tended to shape the technology fuelling the boom, Bollman said.

Rural muscle also relies heavily on the existence of an invisible army of highly skilled and mobile managers willing to work in rural Canada -- a trend at odds with the urban migration patterns of the 1960s and '70s.
Despite the lure of rural Canada, some sceptics wonder whether this boom, like the last one of the late 1980s, will be followed by a bust.

They recall the saga of Schefferville, a once-prosperous mining town in northern Quebec, which produced C$282 million ($208 million) worth of iron in 1979. When the Iron Ore Co. closed the mine in 1983, more than 80 percent of the population slipped away.
The town is now virtually deserted, its remaining residents on welfare.
